problem: It says the top three layers run only on the two end hosts. The internet layer is the exception: IP is implemented in every router as well as in the hosts, and routers read and rewrite the IP header at every hop. Only the application and transport layers are confined to the end hosts.
fix: The application and transport layers run only in the two end hosts. The internet layer runs in the hosts and in every router along the path. The network access layer runs on the hosts and on every device of the link, including switches and access points.

problem: The counts contradict the definition given one line earlier ('end-to-end means the protocol runs only in the two end hosts'). IP is processed by every router in the path, not only by the two end hosts, and ICMP is generated by routers too (destination unreachable, time exceeded). Step 7's own definition, 'runs on every device along the path', therefore also fits IP and ICMP, yet they are left out of the hop-by-hop count. The arithmetic 5+2+2+... = 9 is consistent but the classification is wrong.
fix: End-to-end = runs only in the two end hosts: the 5 application protocols + TCP + UDP = 7. Hop-by-hop = processed at every device on the path: IP, ICMP, Ethernet, Wi-Fi = 4. Boundary: ARP alone = 1. Check: 7 + 4 + 1 = 12. Answer: application 5, transport 2, internet 3, network access 2; 7 protocols work end to end, 4 work hop by hop, and ARP alone sits on the boundary.

problem: QUIC is described as carrying HTTP/3 'with its own reliability built inside the application'. QUIC is normally classed as a transport protocol implemented in user space above UDP; calling it part of the application blurs the layer it is usually placed in, which is exactly what a student will be asked about.
fix: QUIC runs above UDP, in user space, and builds its own reliability and encryption there, so HTTP/3 gets TCP-like delivery without TCP.
